title: Josquin des Prez
wiki_lead:
Josquin Lebloitte dit des Prez (c. 1450 – 1455 – 27 August 1521) was a French or Franco-Flemish composer of Renaissance music. Considered one of the greatest composers of the Renaissance, he was a central figure of the Franco-Flemish School and had a profound influence on 16th-century European music. Building on the work of his predecessors like Johannes Ockeghem, he developed a complex style of expressive, often imitative movement between independent voices (polyphony). He emphasized the relationship between text and music, and departed from the early Renaissance tendency towards lengthy melismatic lines on a single syllable, preferring to use shorter, repeated motifs between voices. Josquin was a singer, and his compositions are mainly vocal. They include masses, motets and secular chansons.
His biography has been continually revised by scholarship. Born in present-day northeastern France or Belgium, he was in the choir of René of Anjou by 1477 and, later, likely served under Louis XI. In the 1480s, Josquin traveled Italy with Cardinal Ascanio Sforza, possibly worked in Vienna for Hungarian king Matthias Corvinus, and wrote the motet Ave Maria ... Virgo serena and popular chansons Adieu mes amours and Que vous ma dame. He served Pope Innocent VIII and Pope Alexander VI, Louis XII, and Ercole I d'Este. Many of his works were printed and published by Ottaviano Petrucci, including the Missa Hercules Dux Ferrariae. In his final years in Condé, Josquin produced some of his most admired works, including the motets Benedicta es, Inviolata, Pater noster–Ave Maria and Praeter rerum seriem, and chansons Nimphes, nappés and Plus nulz regretz.
Described as the first Western composer to retain posthumous fame and influence, Josquin was widely performed and imitated in 16th-century Europe, and was highly praised by Martin Luther and music theorists Heinrich Glarean and Gioseffo Zarlino. In the Baroque era, Josquin was overshadowed by Italian composer Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina. During the 19th- and 20th-century early music revival, publications by August Wilhelm Ambros, Albert Smijers, Helmuth Osthoff, and Edward Lowinsky culminated in a successful academic conference in 1971. This prompted a reevaluation of Josquin as a central figure in Renaissance music, though some scholars have questioned whether he has been unrealistically elevated over his contemporaries. In the 21st century, his music is frequently treated in scholarship and recorded. He was celebrated worldwide on the 500th anniversary of his death in 2021.

Name
Josquin's full name, Josquin Lebloitte dit des Prez, became known in the late 20th century. A pair of 1483 documents found in Condé-sur-l'Escaut identify the composer as the nephew of Gille Lebloitte dit des Prez and the son of Gossard Lebloitte dit des Prez. His first name Josquin is a diminutive form of Josse, the French form of the name of Judoc, a Breton saint of the 7th century. Josquin was a common name in Flanders and Northern France in the 15th and 16th centuries. Other documents indicate that the surname des Prez had been used by the family for at least two generations, perhaps to distinguish them from other branches of the Lebloitte family. At the time, the name Lebloitte was rare and the reason that Josquin's family took up the more common surname des Prez as their dit name remains uncertain.
His name has many spellings in contemporary records: his first name is spelled as Gosse, Gossequin, Jodocus, Joskin, Josquinus, Josse, Jossequin, Judocus and Juschino; and his surname is given as a Prato, de Prato, Pratensis, de Prés, Desprez, des Prés and des Près. In his motet Illibata Dei virgo nutrix, he includes an acrostic of his name, where it is spelled IOSQVIN Des PREZ. Documents from Condé, where he lived for the last years of his life, refer to him as "Maistre Josse Desprez". These include a letter written by the chapter of Notre-Dame of Condé to Margaret of Austria where he is named as "Josquin Desprez"
grok_lead: Josquin des Prez (c. 1450â1521) was a Franco-Flemish composer of the Renaissance, widely regarded as one of the most influential figures in the development of Western polyphonic music. Born around 1450 in the region of modern-day Belgium, near CondÃ©-sur-l'Escaut, he rose to prominence through his mastery of sacred and secular vocal compositions, including masses, motets, and chansons, which emphasized expressive text declamation and innovative contrapuntal techniques. His works, such as the motet Ave Maria... virgo serena and the Missa Pange lingua, exemplify his ability to blend structural rigor with emotional depth, marking a pinnacle of Renaissance musical humanism. Josquin's legacy endures as the "Michelangelo of music," with his compositions shaping the polyphonic tradition and inspiring later masters like Palestrina. Little is known with certainty about Josquin's early life due to sparse documentation, but he likely received musical training as a choirboy in Cambrai around 1466. His career began in the 1470s as a singer in the chapels of RenÃ© of Anjou in Provence and Louis XI of France, before moving to Italy in the 1480s to serve Cardinal Ascanio Sforza in Milan. From 1489 to c. 1495, he held a prominent position in the Papal Chapel in Rome under Popes Innocent VIII and Alexander VI, where he composed many of his most celebrated sacred works amid the vibrant humanist culture of the Vatican. Later appointments included a brief stint at the Este court in Ferrara (1503â1504) and a return to France, culminating in his retirement as provost of the Collegiate Church of Notre-Dame in CondÃ©-sur-l'Escaut, where he died on August 27, 1521. Josquin's musical innovations lie in his sophisticated handling of counterpoint, where multiple independent melodic lines interweave to heighten textual meaning through techniques like word painting and imitation. He composed approximately 18 masses, over 100 motets, and numerous chansons, often drawing on preexisting melodies such as the popular L'homme armÃ© tune for cyclic masses that unified the ordinary sections thematically. In secular works, he infused French chansons with Italianate expressiveness, while his sacred motets, influenced by Renaissance humanism, aimed to evoke virtue and affective response through eloquent musical rhetoric. Despite attribution challengesâmodern scholarship has authenticated only about 103 of over 300 once-attributed piecesâhis oeuvre remains a cornerstone of the Franco-Flemish school, disseminated widely through early prints by Ottaviano Petrucci starting in 1502. Josquin's influence extended across Europe, praised by contemporaries and later by Martin Luther as a divine musician, and his style bridged medieval and modern sensibilities in composition. His emphasis on musica ficta (chromatic alterations for expressive effect) and variational forms paved the way for the High Renaissance's focus on clarity and emotional resonance, ensuring his works' performance and study continue in modern early-music ensembles.
